subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 7-month-old infant is brought for a well-child visit. She rolls over and sits without support, reaches for objects, but is not yet crawling and does not pull to stand. Her parents are worried she is behind because a cousin of the same age is crawling.
question: Which of the following best describes this infant's motor development?

options.text: Delayed, because independent walking should occur by 9 months
Delayed, because crawling should be present by 6 months
Normal, because standing is expected by 7 months even though crawling is not
Normal, because rolling and sitting occur by 6 months, crawling by 8 months, and standing by 10 months
Delayed, because she should be pulling to stand by 7 months

explanation_correct: Gross motor milestones in the infant follow a sequence: lifts head prone by 1 month, rolls and sits by 6 months, crawls by 8 months, stands by 10 months, and walks by 12-18 months. A 7-month-old who rolls and sits is meeting her milestones, and not yet crawling is expected because crawling is achieved by 8 months. Milestone dates are ranges that have been approximated and vary by source. Children not meeting milestones may need assessment for developmental delay, but this infant's examination is normal.

explanation_incorrect.A: Independent walking is expected by 12-18 months, not 9 months, so this expectation is far too early.
explanation_incorrect.B: Crawling is achieved by 8 months, not 6 months; absence of crawling at 7 months is not delayed.
explanation_incorrect.C: Standing is achieved by 10 months, not 7 months; the parent's concern about crawling is unfounded for the wrong reason.
explanation_incorrect.E: Pulling to stand or standing occurs by about 10 months, so it is not expected at 7 months.

educationalObjective: Infant motor milestones progress from rolling/sitting by 6 months to crawling by 8 months and standing by 10 months.
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 6-month-old infant has a normal neurologic examination. On testing, the Moro reflex, rooting reflex, palmar grasp, and Babinski sign are no longer elicitable. The mother asks whether the disappearance of these reflexes is a sign of a problem.
question: Which of the following is the best response?

options.text: It is abnormal because these reflexes should persist throughout infancy
It is normal because primitive reflexes (Moro, rooting, palmar, Babinski) disappear during infancy
It is abnormal because the Babinski sign should remain until 2 years of age
It is a sign of regression to an earlier maturational stage
It is an early indicator of developmental delay

explanation_correct: Primitive reflexes disappear during infancy; the group to know is the Moro, rooting, palmar grasp, and Babinski reflexes, recalled with the mnemonic 'Mr. Peanut Butter.' Their disappearance by around 6 months is a normal part of development as voluntary motor control matures. Milestone dates are approximated ranges and vary somewhat by source. Their appropriate disappearance is a reassuring finding, not a sign of delay or regression.

explanation_incorrect.A: Primitive reflexes are expected to disappear rather than persist throughout infancy; persistence would be the concerning finding.
explanation_incorrect.C: The Babinski sign is one of the primitive reflexes that disappears in infancy; it does not normally persist until age 2 years.
explanation_incorrect.D: Regression is a loss of previously attained abilities under stress, not the normal disappearance of primitive reflexes with maturation.
explanation_incorrect.E: Disappearance of primitive reflexes at this age is a normal maturational event, not evidence of developmental delay.

educationalObjective: Primitive reflexes (Moro, rooting, palmar, Babinski) disappear normally during infancy (Mr. Peanut Butter).
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 7-month-old infant smiles and coos at familiar family members. When an unfamiliar person approaches and reaches for her, she turns away, clings to her mother, and becomes fussy. Her parents worry this behavior is abnormal. She has no other concerns.
question: Which of the following best explains this behavior?

options.text: Stranger anxiety is abnormal before 12 months of age
Separation anxiety normally first appears at 6 months
The social smile normally first appears at 9 months
This pattern strongly suggests autism spectrum disorder
Stranger anxiety normally appears by 6 months, and the social smile by 2 months

explanation_correct: Social milestones include the social smile by 2 months, stranger anxiety by 6 months, and separation anxiety by 9 months. This 7-month-old shows appropriate social smiling and a normal, age-appropriate fear of unfamiliar people. Stranger anxiety is a sign of normal social attachment, not a disorder. The infant's response is therefore expected and reassuring.

explanation_incorrect.A: Stranger anxiety normally emerges by 6 months, so it is entirely expected at 7 months.
explanation_incorrect.B: Separation anxiety normally appears by 9 months, not 6 months; the behavior described is stranger anxiety.
explanation_incorrect.C: The social smile appears by 2 months, not 9 months, and this infant is smiling socially.
explanation_incorrect.D: Normal stranger anxiety and social smiling in a 7-month-old are not indicators of autism spectrum disorder.

educationalObjective: Social smile appears by 2 months, stranger anxiety by 6 months, and separation anxiety by 9 months.
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 10-month-old infant turns when her name is called, searches under a blanket for a toy she watched being hidden, and picks up small cereal pieces neatly between her thumb and forefinger. She babbles 'mama' and 'dada.' She does not yet point to objects.
question: Which combination of milestones is best illustrated by this infant?

options.text: Object permanence by 6 months and pincer grasp by 8 months
Orienting to voice by 9 months and pointing to objects by 10 months
Object permanence and orienting to name and gestures by 9 months, pincer grasp and 'mama/dada' by 10 months
Stranger anxiety by 9 months and social smile by 6 months
Pincer grasp by 12 months and pointing to objects by 10 months

explanation_correct: The infant demonstrates object permanence and orienting to name and gestures, both achieved by 9 months, along with the pincer grasp and saying 'mama' and 'dada,' both achieved by 10 months. Searching for a hidden toy shows object permanence; turning to her name shows orienting to name and gestures. Using thumb and forefinger is the pincer grasp, and her babbling is the oratory milestone. Pointing to objects is achieved by 12 months, so its absence at 10 months is not a concern.

explanation_incorrect.A: Object permanence is achieved by 9 months and the pincer grasp by 10 months, both later than this option states.
explanation_incorrect.B: Orienting to voice occurs by 4 months, not 9 months, and pointing to objects is achieved by 12 months, not 10 months.
explanation_incorrect.D: Stranger anxiety appears by 6 months and the social smile by 2 months, and neither is the main set of skills tested in this vignette.
explanation_incorrect.E: The pincer grasp is achieved by 10 months and pointing by 12 months, so both ages in this option are incorrect.

educationalObjective: By 9-10 months infants show object permanence, orient to name and gestures, use a pincer grasp, and say mama/dada.
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 2-year-old child climbs up the stairs, stacks several blocks into a tower, feeds herself with a fork and spoon, and kicks a ball across the room. She moves away from her parents to explore and then returns to them. Her pediatrician notes that all findings are normal.
question: Which set of milestones best matches this child's abilities?

options.text: Climbs stairs by 18 months, cubes stacked = age (yr) x 3, fork and spoon by 20 months, and kicks ball by 24 months
Climbs stairs by 12 months, cubes stacked = age (yr) x 2, and fork and spoon by 24 months
Takes first steps by 18 months and kicks ball by 36 months
Cubes stacked = age (yr) x 3 equals 9 blocks at 2 years, and fork and spoon by 12 months
Parallel play emerges by 12 months and core gender identity is formed by 24 months

explanation_correct: Toddler milestones (12-36 months) include cruising and first steps by 12 months, climbing stairs by 18 months, stacking a number of cubes equal to age in years multiplied by 3, feeding self with fork and spoon by 20 months, and kicking a ball by 24 months. Rapprochement, moving away from and returning to the parent, occurs by 24 months. This child's skills fit the 18-24 month range. At age 2 years, cubes stacked equals 6, which is consistent with stacking several blocks.

explanation_incorrect.B: Climbing stairs is by 18 months rather than 12, the cube rule is age x 3 rather than x 2, and cutlery use is by 20 months.
explanation_incorrect.C: First steps occur by 12 months and kicking a ball by 24 months, so both ages in this option are too late.
explanation_incorrect.D: At 2 years, age x 3 gives 6 cubes rather than 9, and feeding with fork and spoon is by 20 months rather than 12.
explanation_incorrect.E: Parallel play occurs by 24-36 months and core gender identity forms by 36 months, not 12 and 24 months.

educationalObjective: Toddler milestones include climbing stairs at 18 months, cubes = age x 3, cutlery at 20 months, and kicking a ball at 24 months.
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 4-year-old girl speaks in complete sentences using prepositions and can tell detailed stories about her day. Her 3-year-old brother understands roughly 1000 words and uses more than 300 words. Their pediatrician considers both children's language development normal.
question: Which of the following is consistent with normal language development?

options.text: A 2-year-old should use 300+ words, and a 4-year-old should understand 1000 words
Complete sentences appear by 3 years, and 50-200 words are used by 2 years
A 3-year-old should use 50-200 words, and detailed stories are told by 5 years
50-200 words by 2 years, 300+ words by 3 years, understands 1000 words by 3 years, and complete sentences with prepositions and detailed stories by 4 years
'Mama/dada' is said by 12 months, and 1000 words are understood by 4 years

explanation_correct: Language milestones include 50-200 words by 2 years and 300+ words by 3 years in the toddler period. In the preschool years, children understand 1000 words by 3 years, use complete sentences and prepositions by 4 years, and can tell detailed stories by 4 years. The children described fit these expectations exactly. Note the mnemonic that a 3-year-old understands 1000 words (3 zeros), helping distinguish comprehension from expressive vocabulary.

explanation_incorrect.A: A 2-year-old uses 50-200 words, not 300+, and 1000 words are understood by 3 years rather than first being expected at 4 years.
explanation_incorrect.B: Complete sentences with prepositions appear by 4 years, not 3 years, even though 50-200 words by 2 years is correct.
explanation_incorrect.C: A 3-year-old uses 300+ rather than 50-200 words, and detailed stories are told by 4 years rather than 5 years.
explanation_incorrect.E: 'Mama/dada' is achieved by 10 months rather than 12 months, and 1000 words are understood by 3 years rather than 4 years.

educationalObjective: Language milestones: 50-200 words at 2 years, 300+ at 3 years, 1000 understood at 3 years, complete sentences and stories at 4 years.
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones

subject: Psychiatry
vignette: A 4-year-old child rides a tricycle, copies a circle, hops on one foot, and engages in cooperative play with friends, complete with imaginary friends. He is comfortable spending part of the day away from his parents.
question: Which of the following best characterizes these preschool milestones?

options.text: Tricycle riding at 4 years and hopping on one foot at 5 years
Copies a stick figure by 3 years and uses buttons or zippers by 4 years
Cooperative play by 3 years and comfortable away from parent by 5 years
Hops on one foot by 3 years and rides a tricycle by 5 years
Tricycle by 3 years; hops on one foot, copies a line or circle and stick figure, and shows cooperative play with imaginary friends by 4 years

explanation_correct: Preschool milestones (3-5 years) include driving a tricycle by 3 years, copying a line or circle and a stick figure by 4 years, hopping on one foot by 4 years, and using buttons or zippers and grooming self by 5 years. Comfortably spending part of the day away from a parent occurs by 3 years, while cooperative play and imaginary friends appear by 4 years. This child's abilities match the expected 4-year-old milestones. The '4 on one foot' mnemonic reinforces hopping at age 4.

explanation_incorrect.A: The tricycle is expected by 3 years and hopping on one foot by 4 years, not 4 and 5 years respectively.
explanation_incorrect.B: Copying a stick figure is achieved by 4 years, not 3, and buttons or zippers are used by 5 years, not 4.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cooperative play and imaginary friends appear by 4 years, and being comfortable away from a parent occurs by 3 years, not 3 and 5 years.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hopping on one foot is by 4 years rather than 3, and riding a tricycle is by 3 years rather than 5.

educationalObjective: Preschool milestones: tricycle at 3 years; hopping, copying shapes, and cooperative play with imaginary friends at 4 years.
source: Generated from 13. Psychiatry.pdf - Psychology: Infant and child development milestones
